lesson.title: Knowing When to Stop: Transcription Termination
lesson.summary: Transcription ends when RNA polymerase encounters a specific termination signal in the DNA sequence, which causes the enzyme to release the finished RNA transcript and detach from the DNA.
lesson.body:
Just as the promoter tells RNA polymerase precisely where to start transcribing a gene, as described in the previous chapter, a separate signal located downstream of the gene tells the enzyme precisely where to stop. Without such a signal, RNA polymerase would simply continue transcribing indefinitely, running past the end of the gene and producing RNA from sequences that were never meant to be copied.

In bacteria, two general strategies for termination are well described. In one, sometimes called intrinsic termination, the newly transcribed RNA itself folds back on itself into a hairpin, or stem-loop, structure immediately followed by a run of several uracil (U) bases. This hairpin structure causes RNA polymerase to pause, and the string of weak U-A base pairs holding the RNA to the DNA template at that point is not strong enough to keep the transcript attached under the strain, so the RNA separates from the DNA and RNA polymerase releases the finished transcript and detaches. In the other bacterial strategy, a separate protein factor travels along the newly made RNA behind the polymerase, eventually catching up to it at certain sequences and helping to pull the transcript free from the DNA and enzyme.

In eukaryotic cells, termination for protein-coding genes is closely tied to a specific sequence signal near the end of the gene, the same signal that marks where the poly-A tail will later be added (covered in the mRNA Processing chapter). Recognition of this signal triggers cleavage of the RNA transcript at that site, and this is followed by further events downstream that eventually cause RNA polymerase to lose its grip on the DNA template and stop transcribing.

Regardless of the exact mechanism, the outcome of termination is the same: RNA polymerase releases both the DNA it was transcribing and the finished RNA transcript, which at this point is called the primary transcript. In eukaryotes, this primary transcript is not yet mature messenger RNA. It still needs several finishing modifications, including the addition of a protective cap, the removal of noncoding sequences, and the addition of the poly-A tail whose signal helped trigger termination in the first place, all of which are the subject of the final chapter in this unit.
